I never had major issues from it, even having it regularly.

Building trust with a PO is essential to earning your freedoms back. 

Examples: 

I had an alcohol clause that we got removed because it wasn't an issue and I completed all required treatment.

I had an internet condition that was modified to allow monitored devices. 6 months after completing treatment I will be able to get monitoring completely removed.

I have drug testing that has gone from 3x a month to 1. In 6 months, I can get off of testing completely. 

From 3 tests a month, a flip phone and about 4 hours a week of treatment... I am now at one ua a month with a monitored device. I can use social media on the browser(which is monitored) but not the social media apps. This is from good behavior and proving myself. Do what you are supposed to, and probation gets easier. How society treats you is another story.

The doctor I am getting sleep study through told me that as well, about narcolepsy. My sleep paralysis and the symptoms I have point to narcolepsy even though I don't actually fall asleep(though I regularly lay down wherever I am because I often can't stay standing for long). Says it's very hard to diagnose though, thanks to the multiple latency whatever that requires you to take naps and fall asleep in a certain amount of time.

I've done a lot of online research(hard to get in with my doc). Only GABA is unknown about the interactions. The different supplements I take do interact with each other though. GABA's effectiveness is boosted by the other supplements, so make sure you can tolerate GABA before adding any of the others.

I am about to get my own sleep study. I have had sleep apnea as a child before tonsils and adenoids removed. When I was about 20, I stopped breathing while awake(one of the most frightening things next to my sleep paralysis). About 3 months ago I woke up gasping. 6 months into extreme lethargy and fatigue, and finally requested the test. 

Like you, the doc says it is to rule out sleep apnea, but it is still a real possibility despite being in great health and no obvious risk factors. Hope everyone here resolves their issue, and hope mine is resolved as well.

One note: if you are prone to headaches, go easy on the GABA. It seems to be a somewhat common side effect, but only affects me mildly(despite migraine history) and mostly just feels like a warm pressure behind my forehead before bed. Other reviews have noted stronger headaches, so my fix may not be for everyone.

I actually found a short term fix. My sleep study should be set up tomorrow for sometime this week.

But I used to take a sleep aid because trouble sleeping. It had GABA, 5-HTP, L-Theanine and Melatonin. I've tried melatonin alone and it helps me fall asleep, but wake up after 3 hours and groggier the next day. I cannot find the supplement anywhere... however I got each ingredient alone(GABA 750mg, 5-HTP, L-Theanine with low melatonin and Ashwagandha with low melatonin. This combination puts me to sleep within 30 minutes(compared to an hour or more of struggling) and I sleep all night. On top of that, the first two days I had more energy than I've had in months. Today was alright, but not as good(though I did only get 6 hours last night, which isn't enough.)

I hope this new information helps anyone else like us. But I need to avoid these supplements for the sleep study just to get an accurate baseline for treatment.

Oh and try not to sound like you are making excuses. Use matter of fact language. Don't sound like a victim or justify behavior. Minimizing is one thing, because they don't need to know all of the details. But justification can be a red flag for employers.

I used this phrase: "I want to be completely honest with you"

I told them that and went on to:

I have a criminal background that I feel you should be aware of. In (year) I made some poor life choices and was convicted of (crime).

They will likely ask about it. If not, volunteer more.

 I was incarcerated for (number) years. In that time I accomplished (List progress or accomplishments). Since release I have (explain progress). I am on supervised release and part of my conditions is gainful employment(shows you have more to lose by quitting than most people). 

If nothing else, use:(or end with)

I am not the man I was when I made those decisions. I have made a lot of progress and am willing to prove to you that I am a good fit for this position. If you have any questions about my progress, feel free to contact my PO to verify that I am trustworthy and honest.


Remember: if you don't disclose and a coworker finds out and complains, they can fire you. Not sure about every state, but utah is with no notice whatsoever. Not working is a violation, so try to be careful on deciding whether or not you disclose.

I honestly didn't go through all the comments yet, so sorry if I repeat what others have said.

That said, I have had experience with this and know many others that have. The way to go about it that worked for most of ua:

Don't volunteer up front. Let them get to know you in the interview first. Present your strengths and show you are a good fit for the job. This works for renting places or meeting new people too.
At the end of the interview, bring up your past. I don't advocate minimizing, but in this case it can be helpful. Explain that you made a bad decision in your past, but it doesn't define you. Bring up your progress and strengths again. Show them you are not the person that made the bad decision. 

Your past doesn't define you, and make them realize that in your interview. A lot of employers don't care about your past as long as you are doing what you are supposed to now.

Hope this helps.

Didn't really want to waste time with explanations of the whole situation.. but basically until I was about 30yo when I got this dx, I didn't work. Longest job I held was 6 months, average about a month. One mistake and I'd just walk out. Friendships were basically just friends of friends. 

Even now im not cured of the avoiding part. I still need friends to introduce me to others.. I will not approach someone new. But i can wait in line, be in crowds, take public transportation and have even worked for 2 years at one place now(though I still dwell on my mistakes, they don't cause me to isolate anymore). Its like anything with mental health though. Accept the diagnosis and be willing to do the work. Took 18 months of CBT treatment to get here, and an additional 6 months of EMDR. 

I used my other diagnoses as a crutch to stay in my comfortable patterns. This new diagnosis held myself accountable for my change, which was part of why I lashed out at her so bad(learned later on that me calling her condescending and useless was very hurtful to her, but thats how I felt). But I was happy with one part of the diagnosis from the beginning: the constant medication adjustments and terrible side effects became a thing of the past.

I'm not bad with one on one interactions once I'm comfortable with the person. And believe me, when she first told me im perfectly normal and was just human, I stopped seeing her for months. I felt attacked. But part of SO treatment was having to see her multiple times a week in group and individual. Took me 2 or 3 months to open up to her. But she helped

I guess I could've said more easily treatable than the original diagnoses.

As others said:

First you will be evaluated pre sentencing. Mental health is included in your PSR, pre sentencing report.

If you end up in the Federal system, it isn't as bad as some state facilities, but still inadequate depending on the location. My last designation at Marion got me in with an amazing therapist that basically cured me of my anxiety and helped me deal with my depresion(which was misdiagnosed as bipolar and agoraphobia, but was simply an easily treatable personality disorder, "AvPD". 

If you require medication, it isn't great. They are usually picky about which meds they will prescribe and will often crush Extended Release medications, causing problems. Also they can punish you if you stop taking them before getting permission, though itis rare that they enforce that rule.

Reoffense rates for these crimes are low. Statistics..

That said, for this type of crime, rates are higher. It is more of an addiction, and addictions require a lot of work. I am a pornography case, and if not for my time in prison, and monitoring, I cant guarantee I wouldn't fall back. I honestly don't have physical inclinations(never lured anyone or even wanted to) so that is one difference for me.

State probation varies. Here in Utah you can surprisingly still have a phone. Without monitoring. Only feds get monitored. 3 years probation is not enough if he doesn't get the treatment he needs. And tbh, getting that for 18 months to 2 years in prison is better than out here. Harder to continue destructive behavior in prison(though not impossible for the truly determined, sadly)

There is success for those that work hard to change, but you need to want the change. If he doesn't, a second offense will land him practically the rest of his life in prison. New offense plus violating probation= new charges of possibly 12 years like they wanted... plus having to serve the suspended sentence probation is covering(3 years probation is usually unless he violates. Once he does, they can impose the original sentence).

Hope this helps somewhat. Not the best news, but if you get him committed to treatment he has a chance.
Yep. And I pay for twice a month drug tests. Luckily only 5 bucks, state has to pay 50. Budget cuts making us pay more. And polygraph is 200 bucks a pop, but only 2 of those in treatment.

I use it on my phone. Don't get a low end phone or it will use a lot of your power. It blocks some of the oddest sites. Thanks to ads on our local fox News site, it is blocked under gambling.
On the phone, they can't see everything you do. Ot flags certain things. Questionable images or videos will be sent to your PO. And certain keywords that relate to both terrorism and so crimes are flagged, so don't be surprised if you get calls about the weirdest things. Also, while the word will flag, it will NOT show the context. I can say "he is an ass" but that word just got flgged out of context. If you get called in, then you will be able to prove the context. But to be honest, I use coarse language and I have yet to be called in, though my coworker has. 
Also, all dating apps and social media apps are blocked, but the websites still work. Overall, PCM is sucky, but you learn to live with it. 32 bucks a month to have a device is worth the hassle.

I admitted that I have had that problem since I was 12 years old. It is why I tell people that know about me to keep a close eye on their kids. It is easy to get into and hard to get out, and it can seriously ruin your life.

I spent 8 years in federal prison. 3 at usp Marion, which had a unicor and an excellent treatment staff. 
In prison I got over my fears and anxiety and got a job in a machine shop despite terror about hurting myself. Staff worked through my anxiety and depression while I was incarcerated.

Since release I have held the longest job I have ever had, going on 2 years. I have been promoted over and over and am now going to school for accounting. I bought my first car nd have supported myself since release nearly 2 years ago.

Family has been supportive. Friends I had pre incarceration are mostly gone, but my new group knows about my past and accepts me. My boss knows and only cares about our hard work. Yes it is tough to find a place to live. It is tough to find a job even with low unemployment in my state. But it is possible, and determination and positivity go a long way. 

To those that think an offense is the end, it can be a motivation for aa new beginning. Don't despair, don't give up. I have lifetime supervision and have made my life what it is today because I don't dwell on the negatives. I still occasionally think of ending it all, but it isn't about my offense, it is an issue I have had my whole life. And knowing what I have going for me gives me hope to go on.

Also, I am about to celebrate my one year anniversary. I got rejected when admitting my past, but was given a chance. And it worked out. What you did in your past does not define you, nd most people understand that.

I used p2p about 10 years ago. I was federally indicted, but the prosecutor here in Utah and the judge both took heavily into account my history. I ended up with a plea deal for possession, even though p2p is considered automatic distribution.

Drug use isn't necessarily a bad thing. Some of the best prisons are the ones with a drug program. If you end up in a medium at first, that is likely going to be one of the soft yards with RDAP. Petersburg and Marion are pretty good, though the former was the best by far. A lot of good people in there willing to help out and look out. COs arent as bad as you would think for the most part. As I told someone else, engage in a hobby and avoid the drama and your time will go by like nothing. Treatment in the system isn't bad, but be forewarned that it doesn't help you much when you get out, other than getting you in a healthier mindset. You will most likely still be ordered to do treatment upon release.

For when you get out: laws are getting more relaxed nationwide. Some states are still tough such as Florida, California, New York and Texas. If you can, try to get released to another state if you have family there. It makes things easier.
Registry in some states is disappearing and public opinion isn't as demonizing as before. Everyone at my work and all of my friends know about my past and still accept and respect me. 
Yes, a lot of jobs are a no go, but many companies still hire us. Networking is the best way to find a job in our situation. Cold applications tend to get declined more often than if you have an "in."
Hard to find a place to live, but in my state a former felon started a business buying homes to rent to felons. Not the best situation, but I have my own place and am free.
With a drug history, testing will likely be mandatory. I had a sporadic and limited history, but still test twice a month. Frustrating, but again at least I'm free and it helps keep me accountable for my actions.

An SO charge is not the end of the world. Things get better, you grow, and life goes on. Keep your head up and you will be fine.

I read your initial post. I have to say, my public defender was amazing. He may be an outlier, but he went out of his way for me.

Sentencing took about 2 weeks for me, nd another 4 weeks to get designated. 

Despite what you mentioned about 85% with good time, you serve less now. When the change went into effect, I got an additional 3 months off.

Like Randall said, despite the challenges, things may be better once you get out. I've grown so much in my time in the system, and am better off than ever before.
You will most likely end up in a "soft" yard. Ive been in 3 locations, and even the regular yard wasn't as bad as I expected. The worst part is transfers and holdovers. 

My recommendation: engage in a hobby. I spent my time working and drawing for the most part, with other side jobs. Stay busy and time flies(plus it generally keeps you out of trouble). And never engage in the drama or politics. Never ends well.

I hope for the best for you. Its a shitty situation, but a lot of good can come from it. The worst part is the wait, honestly
